pos: n. (John Holt Rice, 1777–1831, Virginia Presbyterian pastor, editor, and first professor of the seminary at Hampden-Sydney)
biblical_def: John Holt Rice was the Virginia pastor who built a theological seminary out of almost nothing. Converted in his youth, he served country congregations in Charlotte County, then the First Presbyterian Church of Richmond, which he gathered from a handful of worshippers meeting in a borrowed room. He founded the Virginia Evangelical and Literary Magazine and edited it for eleven years, using it to press the churches of the South toward an educated ministry. In 1824 the Synod of Virginia appointed him professor of theology at Hampden-Sydney, and he took the post with one student and no endowment; the institution became Union Theological Seminary. He was offered the presidency of the University of Virginia by Jefferson's board and refused it, judging that a seminary for preachers mattered more than a chair in a university that would have no divinity faculty. He pleaded for Rom 10:14 as a matter of simple arithmetic: a congregation cannot hear without a preacher, and a preacher must be trained. He died worn out at fifty-four, and the seminary he had begun with one student outlived him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education, and a professor as one who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning.
webster_full: SEM'INARY, n. The place or original stock whence any thing is brought or produced; a place of education, in which young persons are instructed in the several branches of learning.
PROFESS'OR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university, college or other seminary.
MIN'ISTER, n. One who serves at the altar; one who performs sacerdotal duties; the pastor of a church, duly authorized or licensed to preach the gospel.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Dan 12:3
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
corruption_summary: A seminary begun with one student and no money, by a man who turned down a university presidency to do it.
corruption_paragraphs: The ordinary modern assumption is that institutions are built by money and that theological education follows prosperity. Rice reversed the order. He raised the seminary by riding to congregations that had never given to anything and asking them for the training of men who would preach to their own grandchildren. Psa 78:6 is the argument he made in print and in the saddle: “That the generation to come might know them” (Psa 78:6).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Rice gave his life to: that a trained ministry is not a luxury of settled churches but the ordinary means by which Rom 10:14 is answered, and that the men who found such schools are rarely the men who enjoy them. He asked for 2Ti 2:15 from his students and gave them little else but books and his own exhausted attention.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim as a herald; orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; kathistemi (G2525), to appoint.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; Romans 10:14.
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, rightly divide; 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to set in order, ordain; Titus 1:5.
Hebrew zahar (H2094) — to shine, to warn; Daniel 12:3.
usage: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the question the seminary answered.
“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — what he required of his one student.
“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — the end for which men were trained.

pos: n. (Stuart Robinson, 1814–1881, Irish-born Kentucky Presbyterian pastor and theologian of the spiritual independence of the church)
biblical_def: Stuart Robinson was born in Ireland, raised in Virginia, and became the clearest American voice for the doctrine that the church is a kingdom of a different order than the state. His book The Church of God as an Essential Element of the Gospel argued that the visible church is not a voluntary society formed by men for religious ends but an institution founded by Christ with its own constitution, officers, and jurisdiction, and that it therefore has no commission to legislate on civil questions. He held the Louisville pulpit, edited the True Presbyterian, and when wartime authorities moved against him he spent four years in Canada rather than submit his pulpit to a political test. He returned and served Louisville until his death. His position was not indifference to public righteousness but a refusal to let the church spend its one commission — Mat 28:19, the teaching of what Christ commanded — on business Christ had not given it. Act 20:27 was his measure of a minister: whether he had declared all the counsel of God, and nothing besides.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the church as a congregation of Christians, and jurisdiction as the legal power of governing within defined limits.
webster_full: CHURCH, n. A congregation of Christians united under one form of ecclesiastical government, in one creed, and using the same ritual and ceremonies.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.
SPIRIT'UAL, a. Consisting of spirit; not material; incorporeal. Pertaining to the renewed nature of man.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: The church is a kingdom with its own charter, and a minister who legislates beyond it has left his commission.
corruption_paragraphs: Robinson wrote against two errors at once, and both are still with us. The first is Erastian: the state assumes authority over the church's worship, officers, and teaching, which is what drove him to Canada. The second is the church's own overreach, in which assemblies bind consciences on matters Scripture has not addressed and then treat dissent as impiety. 1Ti 3:15 names the church “the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — of the truth, which is a bounded commission, not an unbounded one.

The dictionary holds Robinson's principle while refusing the use later made of it. Spiritual independence was invoked in the American South to silence the church on manstealing, which Scripture names outright in the list at 1Ti 1:10 and sentences at Exo 21:16. A doctrine that forbids the church to legislate where Scripture is silent cannot be stretched to forbid her to speak where Scripture is loud. Robinson's rule, honestly applied, obliged the church to preach Exo 21:16; his section of the church did not, and the failure was theirs, not the doctrine's.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), an assembly called out; boule (G1012), counsel, purpose; stulos (G4769), a pillar.
roots_lines: Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out; 1 Timothy 3:15.
Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to make a disciple, to teach; Matthew 28:19.
usage: “the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — the charter, and its limit.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — his measure of a ministry.
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19) — the one commission.

pos: n. (Thomas Smyth, 1808–1873, Irish-born Charleston Presbyterian pastor, controversialist, and defender of the unity of the human race)
etymology: English occupational surname Smith, a worker in metal; the -yth spelling is Irish usage.
biblical_def: Thomas Smyth came from Belfast to Charleston and spent thirty-nine years in the Second Presbyterian Church there, assembling one of the largest private theological libraries in America and writing without pause. His Ecclesiastical Republicanism argued that Presbyterian government, not prelacy, is the New Testament order, reading 1Ti 5:17 and Tit 1:5 as establishing a plurality of ruling elders rather than a single bishop over many congregations. His most durable work was The Unity of the Human Races, written against the Charleston school of ethnologists who were then teaching that mankind descends from several separate creations. Smyth answered from Act 17:26, that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26), and from Rom 5:12, that sin entered by one man and death passed upon all; a plurality of human origins destroys both the imputation of Adam's sin and the one Mediator who answers it. He was mocked locally for the book and pressed it anyway.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unity as the state of being one, and race as the lineage of a family, or descendants of a common stock.
webster_full: U'NITY, n. The state of being one; oneness. Concord; conjunction; agreement; uniformity.
RACE, n. The lineage of a family, or continued series of descendants from a parent who is called the stock. A race is the series of descendants indefinitely.
ELD'ER, n. In the New Testament, an officer in the church, invested with authority to teach or to rule.
scriptures: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
corruption_summary: A Charleston pastor proved the unity of mankind from Scripture while his own city funded the science that denied it.
corruption_paragraphs: The polygenist theory Smyth attacked was not a fringe opinion in Charleston; it carried the prestige of the age's natural science and it was useful to the local economy. Smyth saw what it cost doctrinally. If the nations are not of one blood, then Rom 5:12 has no universal subject, the imputation of Adam's sin collapses, and the gospel is offered to one lineage of men on a ground that cannot reach the rest. His book is a model of refusing a scientific consensus on exegetical grounds and being proved right.

The honest difficulty is that Smyth, having demolished the theory that most directly served slaveholding, did not follow Act 17:26 to its end in his own society. The dictionary names the inconsistency rather than smoothing it. Exo 21:16 sentences the man who steals and sells a man; 1Ti 1:10 lists menstealers with the lawless. A pastor who had just shown all nations to be of one blood owed his congregation that application and withheld it. The lesson is that an argument can be sound and its author still stop short of where it leads.
roots_summary: Greek haima (G129), blood; ethnos (G1484), nation; Hebrew bara (H1254), to create.
usage: “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26) — the text of his best book.
“as by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12) — what polygenism destroys.
“Let the elders that rule well” (1Ti 5:17) — his argument for Presbyterian order.

pos: n. (John Leighton Wilson, 1809–1886, South Carolina Presbyterian, pioneer missionary to West Africa, later secretary of foreign missions)
biblical_def: John Leighton Wilson left South Carolina in 1834 for Cape Palmas and then the Gabon, where he spent nineteen years, reduced the Grebo and Mpongwe tongues to writing, and translated portions of Scripture into both. He is remembered in West Africa chiefly for the report he sent home on the slave trade still running from that coast: he documented the barracoons and the shipments with names and numbers, and his testimony was used in Britain and America against the traffic. He freed the slaves he had inherited in Carolina before he sailed. Ill health brought him back, and from 1861 he served as secretary of foreign missions for the Southern Presbyterian church, keeping a mission enterprise alive through a war that had bankrupted its supporters. Isa 49:6 was his commission, “a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6), and Exo 21:16 was the verse he turned on the trade he found waiting for him at the river mouths.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion, and to kidnap as to steal and carry away a human being.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion. Christian missionaries are of two classes, foreign and domestic.
KID'NAP, v.t. To steal and carry away a human being; particularly, to steal a child.
TRANSL'ATE, v.t. To interpret; to render into another language; to express the sense of one language in the words of another.
scriptures: Isa 49:6

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Psa 82:3
Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.
corruption_summary: He translated Scripture into two African languages and sent home the evidence that the slave trade was still running.
corruption_paragraphs: Wilson's African reports are a case study in what a missionary is for. He had gone to preach, and he did; but he also wrote down what he saw, and what he saw was the continuing export of men from the coast he was evangelizing. His documentation was specific enough to be used against the trade in two countries. Psa 82:3 commands plainly, “Defend the poor and fatherless” (Psa 82:3), and the defence began with an accurate letter.

The corruption to name is the arrangement by which a church sent men abroad to preach deliverance while declining to apply the same texts at home. Wilson himself emancipated his inherited slaves and then served a denomination that defended the institution; he worked inside that contradiction without resolving it. Exo 21:16 is not obscure and does not admit of regional exemption. The dictionary honours the translations and the reports, and names the inconsistency of the sending church as the corruption it was.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'or (H216), light; ganab (H1589), to steal; Greek ktisis (G2937), creature, creation.
usage: “a light to the Gentiles” (Isa 49:6) — the commission he took to the Gabon.
“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — what he found on the coast.
“Defend the poor and fatherless” (Psa 82:3) — why he wrote it all down.

pos: n. (Moses Drury Hoge, 1818–1899, Richmond Presbyterian pastor who ran the blockade to obtain Bibles)
etymology: Surname Hoge, a northern English and Scottish form of Hogg.
biblical_def: Moses Drury Hoge held the Second Presbyterian Church of Richmond for fifty-four years. His best-known act was not a sermon. With the Southern states cut off from the American Bible Society and Scripture growing scarce in the camps and the towns, he sailed through the Federal blockade to Britain in 1862, laid the case before the British and Foreign Bible Society, and obtained a large consignment of Bibles and Testaments, which he brought back through the blockade a second time. He preached to Confederate troops and afterward spent decades rebuilding a ruined city's congregation; he was invited to open the United States Senate in prayer and declined no occasion to urge the reading of Scripture. Isa 55:11 is the text his voyage rested on: the word “shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11), which is a sufficient reason to take great risks to deliver it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a Bible as the book which contains the Scriptures, and a blockade as the shutting up of a place by hostile forces.
webster_full: BIBLE, n. THE BOOK, by way of eminence; the sacred volume, in which are contained the revelations of God, the principles of Christian faith and the rules of practice.
BLOCK'ADE, n. The shutting up of a place by hostile forces, or by troops or ships, to compel a surrender by hunger and want, without regular attacks.
DISTRIB'UTE, v.t. To divide among two or more; to deal out; to give in portions.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
corruption_summary: A pastor twice ran a naval blockade to bring Bibles to people who had none.
corruption_paragraphs: It is worth asking what estimate of Scripture makes such a voyage reasonable. Hoge was not smuggling a symbol. He held that the word of God is “quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12), an instrument that does something when it is read, and that a region without Bibles is a region in real famine. 2Ti 3:15 adds the domestic argument: children are made wise unto salvation by holy scriptures they must actually possess.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the estimate of the Bible that produced the voyage. Where Scripture is abundant it is easily held cheap; Hoge's generation learned its value by scarcity. Act 8:4 records that those who were scattered “went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — the word travels with the people who think it worth carrying.
roots_summary: Hebrew dabar (H1697), word; Greek zao (G2198), living; energes (G1756), powerful, effective.
roots_lines: Greek zao (G2198) — to live, be quick; Hebrews 4:12.
Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to preach good tidings; Acts 8:4.
usage: “it shall not return unto me void” (Isa 55:11) — the warrant for the voyage.
“sharper than any twoedged sword” (Heb 4:12) — why the cargo mattered.
“went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — the word travels with its carriers.

pos: n. (George Howe, 1802–1883, Massachusetts-born professor at Columbia Theological Seminary and historian of Southern Presbyterianism)
etymology: English surname Howe, from Old English hoh, a spur of land, or Old Norse haugr, a hill.
biblical_def: George Howe was born in Massachusetts, trained at Andover, and spent fifty-two years as professor of biblical literature at Columbia Theological Seminary in South Carolina. He taught Hebrew and Greek exegesis to three generations of Southern ministers, and he wrote the History of the Presbyterian Church in South Carolina, two heavy volumes assembled from session books, presbytery minutes, and the memories of old men, which preserved records that would otherwise have burned or rotted. He defended the historic authorship of the Pentateuch and of Isaiah against the German criticism then entering American divinity schools, holding with the dictionary that Moses wrote the Torah and that one prophet Isaiah wrote the book bearing his name. His labour was unglamorous: languages, documents, and dates. Pro 18:15 describes the temper of it, “The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge” (Pro 18:15), and Psa 78:4 names the end, that the works of the LORD not be hidden from the children.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of facts in the order of time, and exegesis as explanation, exposition.
webster_full: HIST'ORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states; a narration of events in the order in which they happened, with their causes and effects.
EXEGE'SIS, n. Exposition; explanation; interpretation.
REC'ORD, n. A register; an authentic or official copy of any writing, or account of any facts and proceedings, entered in a book for preservation.
scriptures: The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
corruption_summary: Fifty-two years of Hebrew, Greek, and session books, so that a church would know its own past.
corruption_paragraphs: Howe's history was written against forgetting, which is a church's ordinary condition. Congregations lose their own records within two generations, and with the records goes the memory of what was contended for and why. Psa 78:4 makes the transmission a duty: “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4). A man who copies out presbytery minutes for twenty years is obeying that verse in a form nobody applauds.

He taught exegesis in the decades when the documentary hypothesis and the division of Isaiah were being imported from Germany as the mark of a modern divinity faculty, and he resisted both. The dictionary holds his position: Mosaic authorship of the Torah, one Isaiah, no Deutero-Isaiah and no Priestly source. Luk 24:27 is the reason it matters — Christ expounded “in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27), treating the books as the books the church had received.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (H995), to discern; kachad (H3582), to hide; Greek diermeneuo (G1329), to expound.
roots_lines: Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, be prudent; Proverbs 18:15.
usage: “The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge” (Pro 18:15) — the temper of his work.
“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — why he wrote the history.
“in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27) — the exegete's rule.

pos: n. (Robert Jefferson Breckinridge, 1800–1871, Kentucky Presbyterian, Old School controversialist and theologian)
etymology: Scottish-Irish surname Breckinridge, from a place name meaning the speckled ridge.
biblical_def: Robert J. Breckinridge left the law and the Kentucky legislature for the ministry and became one of the hardest-hitting controversialists of the Old School Presbyterian party. He edited the Baltimore Literary and Religious Magazine, led the prosecution of theological laxity in the 1837–38 division, served as superintendent of public instruction in Kentucky, and taught at the Danville seminary he helped found. His two volumes, The Knowledge of God Objectively Considered and Subjectively Considered, are a systematic theology of the strict Calvinist kind, built on the twin facts of God's eternal purpose and man's inability. He fought Roman claims in public debate and he fought the New Haven modifications of original sin with the same vigour. Rom 9:16 was his shortest answer to both, that it is “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines controversy as a disputation, particularly in writing, and objective as belonging to the object, in distinction from subjective.
webster_full: CONTROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions. A dispute is commonly oral, and a controversy in writing.
OBJECT'IVE, a. Belonging to the object; contained in the object. Objective certainty is when the proposition is certainly true in itself.
SUBJECT'IVE, a. Relating to the subject, as opposed to the object; arising from within.
scriptures: Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Rom 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
corruption_summary: A lawyer turned theologian who fought Rome and the New Haven men with the same text.
corruption_paragraphs: Breckinridge is a useful figure because he treated two very different errors as one error. Roman theology lodges a share of salvation in the sinner's cooperation administered through the church; the New Haven theology of his own country lodged it in the sinner's unimpaired power of choice. Both leave the decisive act with man. Rom 9:16 forecloses it, and Rom 8:7 explains why: “the carnal mind is enmity against God” (Rom 8:7), and is “not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7).

His manner was severe and he made enemies inside his own party, which is the ordinary cost of judicial prosecution in a church court. The dictionary does not treat polemic as a defect. Gal 1:8 sets the precedent that another gospel is to be named accursed rather than conversed with, and the Old School men who divided the denomination in 1837 were doing what Eph 1:4 required of them: refusing to let election be reduced to a divine response to foreseen choice.
roots_summary: Greek eleeo (G1653), to show mercy; eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; phronema (G5427), the mind, the bent of thought.
roots_lines: Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to wish; Romans 9:16.
Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out, elect; Ephesians 1:4.
Greek phronema (G5427) — the mind, its bent; Romans 8:7.
Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.
usage: “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — his answer to Rome and New Haven alike.
“the carnal mind is enmity against God” (Rom 8:7) — the ground of inability.
“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — the warrant for polemic.

pos: n. (Charles Colcock Jones, 1804–1863, Georgia Presbyterian minister and plantation catechist)
etymology: English patronymic Jones, son of John; Colcock a Carolina family name.
biblical_def: Charles Colcock Jones was a Liberty County, Georgia, planter who trained at Andover and Princeton and returned to spend his life catechizing the slaves of the Georgia low country. He preached to them on three plantations in rotation, wrote A Catechism of Scripture Doctrine and Practice for oral use with people forbidden to read, organised watchmen and classes drawn from among them, and published The Religious Instruction of the Negroes in the United States to press other owners to the same work. He taught at Columbia Seminary and served as secretary of the Presbyterian board of domestic missions. He was called in his own circles the apostle to the slaves, and the catechism he wrote was used for decades. He also owned the people he catechized, and freed none of them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers, and to catechize as to instruct by asking questions and correcting the answers.
webster_full: CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
CATECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
MEN'STEALER, n. One who steals men; one who kidnaps.
scriptures: And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
Deu 24:7
If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you.
Woe unto him that buildeth his house by unrighteousness, and his chambers by wrong; that useth his neighbour's service without wages, and giveth him not for his work;
corruption_summary: He taught the catechism to people he refused to free, and the catechism he taught condemned him.
corruption_paragraphs: Jones is the clearest case in American church history of a genuine religious labour built on an institution Scripture condemns outright. The instruction was real; so were the watchmen, the classes, and the forty years of riding between plantations. But Exo 21:16 fixes a capital penalty on the man who steals and sells a man, Deu 24:7 repeats it for Israel, and 1Ti 1:10 lists menstealers in the same breath as the lawless and the perjured. Jer 22:13 pronounces woe on him who “useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13), which is the plantation arrangement in six words.

The dictionary refuses both of the usual evasions. The first calls Jones a man of his time, as though the texts were unavailable to his time; he had Hebrew and Greek and read both. The second treats his catechetical work as cancelling the wrong, when in fact it aggravates it: he taught these people that God requires justice and withheld it from them himself. The lesson for the reader is that sincerity, industry, and sound doctrine on paper can coexist with a settled, defended, lifelong sin, and that the church which honoured him failed to put Exo 21:16 to him plainly.
roots_summary: Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal; Greek andrapodistes (G405), a slave-dealer, menstealer; Hebrew sakar (H7939), wages.
usage: “he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — the law he never applied to himself.
“for menstealers, for liars” (1Ti 1:10) — the company Paul assigns.
“useth his neighbour's service without wages” (Jer 22:13) — the woe pronounced.

pos: n. (Daniel Baker, 1791–1857, Presbyterian evangelist in the American South and Southwest, founder of Austin College)
etymology: English occupational surname Baker, one who bakes.
biblical_def: Daniel Baker was orphaned in Georgia, worked his way through Hampden-Sydney and Princeton, and after settled pastorates in Washington and Savannah gave the rest of his life to itinerant evangelism. He rode the South and then the Texas frontier, holding protracted meetings in courthouses, barns, and camp grounds, and preaching the same plain doctrine everywhere: that man is dead in sins, that God quickens whom He will, and that the hearer is commanded to repent and believe now. He was a revivalist without the New Haven theology; his preaching assumed Eph 2:1, that his hearers were “dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1), and therefore pressed conversion as a work of God rather than a decision within the sinner's unaided reach. He founded Austin College in 1849 and raised its funds himself by preaching. He is the type of the frontier evangelist whose doctrine was Calvinist and whose urgency was total.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an evangelist as a preacher of the gospel, and a revival as a renewal of attention to religion, after indifference.
webster_full: EVAN'GELIST, n. A writer of the history or doctrines, precepts, actions and death of Jesus Christ; a preacher or publisher of the gospel of Jesus Christ.
REVI'VAL, n. Renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline. Revival of letters, the recurrence of attention to learning.
QUICK'EN, v.t. To make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death or an inanimate state.
scriptures: Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Act 2:38
Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
corruption_summary: A frontier evangelist whose urgency never cost him the doctrine of inability.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual assumption is that urgent evangelism requires Arminian machinery — that if a man truly believes sinners are dead, he will not press them. Baker's career is the counter-example. He preached Eph 2:5, that God “hath quickened us together with Christ” (Eph 2:5), and from that very doctrine took his boldness: if conversion is God's act, the preacher is free to plead with everyone, since he is not manufacturing the result.

The corruption to name is the anxious-bench technique that spread in his lifetime and has never left, in which the measures themselves are trusted to produce the new birth. Joh 6:44 forbids the confidence: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44). Baker called men to repent and be baptized as Act 2:38 does, and left the drawing to God. The modern invitation system frequently reverses this and treats a procedure as the agent.
roots_summary: Greek zoopoieo / suzoopoieo (G4806), to quicken together; helko (G1670), to draw; metanoeo (G3340), to repent.
roots_lines: Greek suzoopoieo (G4806) — to quicken together with; Ephesians 2:5.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to repent, change the mind; Acts 2:38.
usage: “dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — what he assumed of every hearer.
“hath quickened us together with Christ” (Eph 2:5) — the ground of his boldness.
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you” (Act 2:38) — the command he pressed.

pos: n. (James Waddel Alexander, 1804–1859, Princeton professor, pastor, and translator of Latin and German hymns)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Waddel from his grandfather, the blind preacher James Waddel.
biblical_def: James Waddel Alexander was the eldest son of Archibald Alexander and the brother of Joseph Addison Alexander. He pastored in Trenton and in New York, edited the Presbyterian, and taught church history and then rhetoric at Princeton Seminary. He is remembered for two things. The first is Thoughts on Preaching, published after his death from his notebooks, a book of hard sayings about the pulpit that ministers have quoted ever since: that the preacher's business is the text and the people before him, not his own figure. The second is his English version of the Latin hymn attributed to Bernard, “O Sacred Head, Now Wounded,” made from the German of Gerhardt, which carried that passion hymn into English-speaking worship. His own measure of a sermon was 2Ti 4:2 taken whole — preach, be instant, reprove, rebuke, exhort, and do it with longsuffering and doctrine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hymn as a song or ode in honor of God, and preaching as the act of pronouncing a discourse on a religious subject.
webster_full: HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity. A hymn among Christians is a short poem, composed for religious service.
PREACH'ING, n. The act of preaching; a public religious discourse.
RHET'ORIC, n. The art of speaking with propriety, elegance and force.
scriptures: Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
Psa 96:3
Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people.
corruption_summary: His book on preaching and his translation of a passion hymn outlived everything else he wrote.
corruption_paragraphs: Thoughts on Preaching is chiefly an attack on the preacher's vanity, and its usefulness has not dated. Alexander held that the work is announcement, not display, which is what 1Co 1:21 establishes: it pleased God “by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). The means is deliberately unimpressive, and a preacher who tries to make it impressive is working against it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pairing in 2Ti 4:2, where reproof and rebuke are commanded in the same clause as longsuffering: “reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2). Pulpits tend to keep one half. Alexander's hymn translation shows the other side of the same man — that the sharpest instructor of preachers spent his spare hours putting a medieval passion hymn into singable English.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering; noutheteo (G3560), to warn, admonish.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; 2 Timothy 4:2.
Greek kerugma (G2782) — the thing preached, proclamation; 1 Corinthians 1:21.
usage: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — his whole rule for the pulpit.
“by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) — why display is self-defeating.
“warning every man, and teaching every man” (Col 1:28) — the pastoral reach of a sermon.
